A gerund is a noun made from a verb by adding "-ing". You can use a gerund as the subject, the complement, or the object of a sentence.

The infinitive is the base form of a verb - “to + verb”.

A gerund is an action verb that is acting as a noun. The noun refers to an activity instead of a person or thing. Gerunds are written in their -ing form.You can use a gerund as the subject, the complement, or the object of a sentence.

Example:
Reading helps your comprehension and vocabulary. (subject of sentence)
Justin's favorite pastime is reading. (complement of sentence)
He enjoys reading. (object of sentence)
An infinitive is a verb form that acts as other parts of speech in a sentence. It is formed with to + base form of the verb.
Example: to talk, to enjoy, to play
You cannot add s, es, ed, or ing to the end. It is not a verb.

You write a resume to give a potential employer an understanding of your education, work experience, credentials and accomplishments. It is a very important piece of a job application.

Your resume should look professional. Don't make it too long.
Employers generally prefer that a resume fits on one page.

A resume should include:
  • Name and contact information
  • Objective or summary statement (This means that you explain what type of position you're looking for and your employment goals)
  • Work experience
  • Volunteer and extracurricular experience
  • Education
  • Skills
When you write a resume, only include clear, short descriptions. You do not have to write full sentences.
You should adjust your resume each time you apply for a position. A resume should feature the items that are most important for the position.
Make sure to add new experiences and skills to keep your resume current.
Example: Make sure that your cover letter and resume are polished.

Susan: Thanks for meeting with me. I'd really love to hear your thoughts on the advertised position.
Sally: No problem.
Susan: When I saw your e-mail this morning about Paul's termination and the job vacancy, I was a little surprised.
Sally: It was a bit of a shock to all of us. Working at Cambridge Life meant everything to him. We were told by the Executive Director last week. Anyway, I thought you might be interested in applying. You're still at The Valley News, aren't you?
Susan: Yes, I worked there as a senior reporter for two years. I'm also completing an MBA, part-time.

Sally: A Master in Business Administration? Are you planning to change positions one day?
Susan: Actually, I want to move into management.
Sally: I see. Paul was part of the management team. It was also mentioned by a few of the senior editors that he was a jack of all trades.
Susan: This position might be a great opportunity for me to get my hands dirty. Currently, I'm working on improving my resume. The deadline is this Friday.

Sally: Could you start working right away if you needed to? It's pretty hectic at the moment.
Susan: Well ... I do have to give my current employer a resignation letter and 2 weeks' notice. That's what I was told by the lawyer when I signed my contract.
Sally: I see.
Susan: Will you put in a good word for me?
Sally: Absolutely! Make sure that your cover letter and resume are polished. Starting with your work objectives followed by your relevant work experience is important ... and watch your spelling!
Susan: Thanks for your help.
